To endue someone with something means to provide them with, invest them with, or equip them with a quality, ability, power, or characteristic — especially one that comes from an outside source rather than something they developed on their own.

Think of it this way: when someone is endued with a quality, it is as if that quality is placed into them or wrapped around them — almost like a garment they are clothed with. In fact, the word carries a strong sense of being furnished or supplied with something, not earning it yourself.
The Shape of How It's Used

The word almost always follows this pattern:

Someone is endued with [a quality/power/attribute]

The person receiving the quality is the focus, and the quality itself is usually something abstract and significant — like wisdom, power, grace, courage, strength, virtue, or a special gift.

Examples:

  • She was endued with extraordinary patience.
  • The king was endued with wisdom beyond his years.
  • He felt endued with a strange new confidence after the experience.
  • The spirit endued the disciples with power.

Notice that in these sentences, the person doesn't acquire the quality through effort or practice. Instead, it is given to them — bestowed upon them by God, nature, fate, circumstances, or some higher force.

The word carries a particular tone that sets it apart from everyday synonyms like "give" or "have."

When you say "She has patience," it is a flat, neutral observation.

When you say "She was endued with patience," it suggests that her patience is not merely a personality quirk — it is almost a gift, something deep and substantial that has been placed within her, something that defines and elevates her.

There is a slight sense of dignity and weight to the word. It implies the quality is meaningful, not trivial. You would never say someone was endued with the ability to whistle — the word feels right when the quality being given is something important, profound, or powerful.

One of the richest ways to understand endue is through the image of clothing. Just as a garment wraps around you and becomes part of how you appear and move through the world, a quality that you are endued with wraps around you — it becomes an integral part of who you are and how you operate.

This is why you will often find the word used in religious, spiritual, or literary contexts, where writers want to convey that a person has been clothed in something higher — power, holiness, grace, strength.

"Be endued with power from on high" — this is the kind of sentence where the word feels perfectly at home.

More often than not, the source of the quality is either:

  • God or a divine force — spiritual gifts, power, grace
  • Nature — natural gifts, innate abilities
  • Circumstances or experience — a situation that equips someone
  • A vague higher authority — "fate endued him with..."

This is why the word tends to appear in elevated writing, classical literature, religious texts, and formal prose. In casual conversation, you would almost never hear it — someone wouldn't say "My sister is endued with great cooking skills." That would sound oddly formal.
How It Differs from Its Nearest Synonyms

Endow — The closest synonym. "Endow" and "endue" are nearly interchangeable. However, "endow" is far more common in modern English, while "endue" sounds more literary and archaic. Both carry the same idea of being furnished with a quality from an outside source.

Bestow — To bestow is to give a gift. The focus is on the act of giving. With endue, the focus is on what the person now possesses as a result — the quality becomes part of them.

Invest (older meaning) — In older usage, to invest someone with authority or qualities is very close to endue. Both carry the idea of placing something upon a person.

Grant — More transactional; it implies permission or a formal transfer. Endue is deeper — it is about a quality being woven into someone's character or being.
Register and Tone: When Would You Actually Encounter This Word?

You will encounter endue primarily in:

  • Classic literature (Shakespeare, Milton, the King James Bible, 18th and 19th-century writing)
  • Religious and theological texts
  • Formal or ceremonial writing
  • Poetry and elevated prose

In modern everyday English, the word is rare. Writers who use it today are usually making a deliberate choice to invoke a sense of gravity, formality, or timelessness. If you come across it while reading, it almost always signals that the writer wants you to feel the weight and significance of the quality being described.

If you ever want to recall this word instantly, remember:

Endue = to clothe someone in a quality they have been given.

Not a quality they built. Not a quality they bought. A quality that was placed into them — as if they were dressed in it from the outside, and now wear it as their own.
